purpose: Execution of chapter 3 of the UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts (2016 edition): general provisions on validity (art. 3.1.1–3.1.4), the grounds for avoidance — mistake, fraud, threat, gross disparity, third persons — and the effects of avoidance (art. 3.2.1–3.2.17), and illegality of a contract infringing a mandatory rule (art. 3.3.1, 3.3.2). The types for party, contract, term and the organ of evaluative elements come from the hub `unidroit.picc`. The package answers exactly where the 1980 UN Convention declines to answer (article 4(a)). The list of questions and boundaries is in analysis/questions.json and QUESTIONS.md.
limitations: THIS IS NOT THE LAW OF A STATE. The Principles apply when the parties have agreed on them, or when a court or arbitral tribunal takes them as general principles of law; they do not replace the mandatory rules of the applicable law (article 1.4, hub `unidroit.picc`).

HERE THE CONVENTION IS SILENT BY ITS OWN DECLARATION: article 4(a) takes the validity of the contract and of its provisions out of its subject matter. Chapter 3 of the Principles answers where the Convention declines to, and in substance there is no bridge between them.

THE CHAPTER DOES NOT DEAL WITH CAPACITY (article 3.1.1): the conditions of a party's capacity are a question of the applicable law and an input of the case. The model answers this with a boundary rather than a conclusion.

THE EVALUATIVE ELEMENTS OF CHAPTER 3 GO THROUGH THE §47.3 JUDGMENT CHANNEL with the organ `Tribunal`: whether a reasonable person would have made the mistake material (3.2.2), a departure from reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing (3.2.2), the imminence and gravity of a threat (3.2.6), an excessive and unjustified advantage (3.2.7), a reasonable time for notice (3.2.12), the unreasonableness of upholding the remaining contract (3.2.13), a reasonable allowance in money (3.2.15), the reasonableness of remedies and of restitution in the case of illegality (3.3.1, 3.3.2). The model neither decides them nor substitutes a guess.

WHICH RULE IS MANDATORY AND WHAT IT PRESCRIBES IS AN INPUT OF THE CASE: article 3.3.1 refers to the infringed rule itself, and the Principles step in only where it is silent. Neither the list of such rules nor their effects is carried into the model.

THE LISTS OF FACTORS IN ARTICLES 3.2.7 AND 3.3.1 ARE NOT EXHAUSTIVE ("among other factors", "in particular"): the seven criteria of article 3.3.1(3) and the two factors of article 3.2.7 are named in the request for a judgment rather than spread into separate premises — otherwise the model would pass off its own completeness as the rule.
